# Further Reading {#sec-further-reading}

Short and annotated. The chapters cite everything they use; these are the sources most
worth reading in full.

## Textbooks

- Jorge Nocedal and Stephen Wright, *Numerical Optimization* [@nocedal2006numerical]:
  the standard reference for gradient, Newton, quasi-Newton, conjugate-gradient and
  constrained methods, with proofs and practical advice. The source for most of
  @sec-gradient-methods.
- Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, *Convex Optimization* [@boyd2004convex]:
  convexity, duality and interior-point methods, with many modeling examples. Free
  online. The source for most of @sec-constraints.
- Steven Brunton, *Optimization Bootcamp* [@brunton2026optimization]: a lecture series
  covering much of this book's ground with an applied, visual emphasis; it was the
  starting point for this project.
- Christopher Bishop, *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning* [@bishop2006pattern]:
  maximum likelihood, the Laplace approximation and EM, as used in @sec-estimation.
- Carl Rasmussen and Christopher Williams, *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning*
  [@rasmussen2006gaussian]: the surrogate model behind Bayesian optimization.
- George Dantzig, *Linear Programming and Extensions* [@dantzig1963linear]: the origin of
  the simplex method, by its inventor.

## Papers worth reading in full

- Stephen Boyd and coauthors on ADMM [@boyd2011distributed]: a long, readable survey of
  splitting methods and their applications.
- Amir Beck and Marc Teboulle on FISTA [@beck2009fast]: proximal gradient and its
  accelerated version, with clear proofs.
- Donald Jones, Matthias Schonlau and William Welch on efficient global optimization
  [@jones1998efficient]: the paper that made Bayesian optimization with expected
  improvement standard.
- Yann Dauphin and coauthors on saddle points [@dauphin2014identifying], and Hao Li and
  coauthors on visualizing loss landscapes [@li2018visualizing]: two entry points to the
  questions of @sec-high-dim.
- Arthur Jacot, Franck Gabriel and Clément Hongler on the neural tangent kernel
  [@jacot2018neural]: why very wide networks train like linear models.
